blocks.content: Meghalaya's demography chapter is dominated by one of its most distinctive and frequently tested social features: the Khasi and Garo communities' matrilineal social system, one of the world's largest surviving matrilineal societies — a system worth understanding in structural detail, not just as a passing fact.

cells: approx 86% — one of the highest ST population shares of any Indian state
approx 75% — Meghalaya is one of only a small number of Christian-majority Indian states
approx 989 females per 1,000 males — among the more favourable sex ratios of Indian states

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Meghalaya's ST population share (~86%) is among the highest of any Indian state, and its Christian population share (~75%) makes it one of only a handful of Christian-majority states in India — both frequently tested superlative/comparative demographic facts.

cells: Meghalaya's largest single tribal community; matrilineal; speak Khasi, an Austroasiatic (Mon-Khmer branch) language — linguistically distinct from most of the rest of North-East India's predominantly Tibeto-Burman-speaking tribes
Closely related to the Khasi in language and matrilineal social structure, though often treated as a culturally and administratively distinct community with its own traditions

Meghalaya's second-largest tribal community; also matrilineal; speak Garo, a Tibeto-Burman language — LINGUISTICALLY DISTINCT from the Austroasiatic Khasi/Jaintia languages, despite sharing the matrilineal social system

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Khasi/Jaintia languages (Austroasiatic, Mon-Khmer branch) and Garo language (Tibeto-Burman) belong to ENTIRELY DIFFERENT language families, despite both communities sharing matrilineal social organisation — a frequently tested linguistic-classification fact that cuts across the shared-matriliny generalisation.

Among both the Khasi and Garo communities, family lineage, clan membership, and inheritance of property pass through the MOTHER's line rather than the father's — children take their mother's clan name, and, distinctively, the YOUNGEST daughter ('Ka Khadduh' in Khasi tradition) customarily inherits the ancestral family property and home, taking on responsibility for caring for aging parents and maintaining ancestral rites.

Despite this matrilineal inheritance and lineage system, it is important to note (a frequently tested nuance) that Khasi and Garo societies are NOT matriarchal in the sense of women holding formal political/public authority — traditional political institutions (the Khasi Hima/Syiem system, Chapter 2; Garo Nokma system) have historically been predominantly male-led, meaning descent/inheritance and political authority operate along different lines — a distinction candidates should not conflate.

In recent decades, a notable social movement — most prominently articulated through organisations such as the 'Syngkhong Rympei Thymmai' (SRT) — has campaigned for reform of the matrilineal system, particularly advocating for greater recognition of men's roles and responsibilities within the family structure; this reform movement is a genuine, actively discussed contemporary social debate within Khasi society rather than a universally settled matter.

★ EXAM POINT: Matrilineal (property/lineage through the mother) does NOT mean matriarchal (women holding formal political authority) — Khasi/Garo traditional political institutions have historically been predominantly male-led. This distinction is one of the most important nuances tested in questions about Meghalaya's social structure.

items: Population (2011): approx 29.67 lakh; ST share approx 86%; Christian share approx 75% (one of India's few Christian-majority states).
Three main communities: Khasi (largest, Khasi Hills), Jaintia/Pnar (Jaintia Hills), Garo (2nd largest, Garo Hills) — all practise matrilineal inheritance.
Khasi/Jaintia languages = Austroasiatic (Mon-Khmer); Garo language = Tibeto-Burman — different families despite shared matriliny.
Matrilineal system: youngest daughter ('Ka Khadduh' in Khasi tradition) customarily inherits ancestral property; NOT matriarchal — political institutions have historically been male-led.
Syngkhong Rympei Thymmai (SRT) = a notable contemporary movement advocating reform of the matrilineal system.
